name: Protect now
plain_question: How do we protect children, workers and people with few choices while the air is still dirty?
theory_of_change: Emission cuts take years. In the meantime, protection that works through existing services (schools, welfare boards, health systems, employers) can reduce exposure and income shocks for those who cannot avoid them, provided it is measured and does not replace source control.
who_changes_what: Welfare boards register and pay idled workers; schools teach protective behaviour; employers and municipalities supply fitted respirators and adjust shifts; health departments prepare for episodes.
capital_form: Philanthropy for outreach, measurement and design; public budgets for transfers and services
cost_order_of_magnitude: Costing required (transfers are public; outreach costs not sourced)
prerequisites: Legal duties exist (court orders, OSH Code, NAMASTE); data access to boards
owner_of_operations: Welfare boards; school systems; municipal employers
evidence_available: Restriction income loss (Strong); school education RCT (Moderate); occupational impairment (Moderate)
evidence_thin: Respirator adherence; purifier health effect; informal earnings loss
decisive_questions: Does registration help raise the share of idled workers paid within 30 days?
learning_agenda_12_24m: Staggered registration rollout with board data; respirator pilot with personal monitors; second-site school trial
risks_and_distribution: Protection can shift attention from source control; costs may fall on workers if PPE is unpaid
local_partner_roles: Worker unions, waste-picker collectives, school systems
exit_and_sustainability: Boards and departments absorb outreach and running costs
what_would_change_my_mind: If paid share does not rise after two seasons, or purifiers keep underperforming education alone

name: Measure the invisible
plain_question: Who is breathing what, where official monitors do not reach, and does the data change decisions?
theory_of_change: Most districts have no government monitor. Calibrated low-cost and community monitoring can make exposure visible, but only changes outcomes when a named authority commits to act on it.
who_changes_what: Regulators accept calibrated data; communities and workers measure hotspots; agencies publish data with response protocols.
prerequisites: Calibration against reference monitors; a regulator willing to respond
evidence_available: Monitoring gaps (Strong); exceedances found by volunteers (reported)
evidence_thin: Whether data triggers action; sensor accuracy at very high concentrations
decisive_questions: Which data led to a documented enforcement or service change?
learning_agenda_12_24m: Co-location calibration; a written response protocol in two districts; log of actions triggered
risks_and_distribution: Data can be dismissed or used to stigmatise communities
what_would_change_my_mind: If no documented action follows within 18 months of data release

name: Make the polluting economy cleaner
plain_question: Can kilns, small industry, farms and transport cut emissions without pushing costs onto workers?
theory_of_change: Cleaner technology exists for kilns, boilers, residue and buses, but adoption depends on credit, markets and enforcement, and workers rarely share in the gains unless conditions are attached.
who_changes_what: Owners and farmers adopt cleaner technology with finance; buyers create residue markets; governments set and enforce standards; labour safeguards attach to transition finance.
capital_form: Concessional and commercial finance; public budgets; philanthropy for worker safeguards and evaluation
cost_order_of_magnitude: Large (World Bank programmes US$52-300m each, approved); costing required for worker components
evidence_available: Kiln emission savings (Moderate); fire-count declines (attribution unclear)
evidence_thin: Worker pay and debt after transition; residue-market durability; street-level effect of e-buses
decisive_questions: Do workers' pay records, debt and exposure improve after conversion?
learning_agenda_12_24m: Matched comparison of converted and unconverted kilns over one season; residue-market price tracking
risks_and_distribution: Bondage and job losses; smallholders excluded from machinery
exit_and_sustainability: Markets and regulation sustain change after subsidies
what_would_change_my_mind: If conversion leaves worker conditions unchanged or worse

name: Build the public systems
plain_question: Do governments have the plans, staff, data and budgets to deliver clean air across an airshed?
theory_of_change: Pollution crosses city and state lines. Airshed plans, monitoring, procurement and enforcement capacity are public goods that make every other investment work; philanthropy and technical assistance can help build them and track delivery.
who_changes_what: States coordinate airshed plans; agencies track spending and results; independent evaluators test measures before scale.
capital_form: Technical assistance; public budgets; philanthropy for independent evaluation
cost_order_of_magnitude: TA in the low millions (ADB TA ~US$4.1m listed sources); costing required otherwise
evidence_available: Upwind transport and cost-effectiveness of coordinated action (modelled); evaluation that stopped smog towers
evidence_thin: Whether plans are delivered and funded; fund utilisation
decisive_questions: Which plan measures are funded, delivered and measured each year?
learning_agenda_12_24m: Annual public tracker of plan delivery; two independent evaluations of large measures
what_would_change_my_mind: If governments refuse data access or ignore findings

name: Fund locally led action
plain_question: Who speaks for the people most exposed, and do they have resources to act?
theory_of_change: Workers, waste pickers, women's groups and health professionals hold knowledge and legitimacy that official systems lack. Funding their organising can unlock entitlements and accountability, if outcomes are measured and voices are not tokenised.
who_changes_what: Community and worker organisations gain resources; authorities create channels to respond; funders measure outcomes, not outputs.
prerequisites: Organisations with legitimacy; safety for workers who speak up
evidence_available: Outputs reported by funders; no independent outcome evaluation
evidence_thin: Effect on entitlements received and policies changed
decisive_questions: Did organising increase benefits received or change a decision?
learning_agenda_12_24m: Outcome tracking alongside outputs; independent review of two grants
risks_and_distribution: Tokenism; dependence on grants; retaliation against workers
exit_and_sustainability: Membership dues; public contracts for outreach
what_would_change_my_mind: If outcomes stay unmeasured after two years

name: Create investable pathways
plain_question: How does a grant-funded pilot become a public programme or a financed market?
theory_of_change: Philanthropy proves a concept; technical assistance designs it into policy or procurement; public or concessional finance scales it; stable operations and maintenance keep it running. Each step needs a different kind of capital.
who_changes_what: Funders sequence capital: grants for proof, TA for design, public or concessional finance for scale, budgets or user payments for operations.
capital_form: Sequenced: grants → TA → concessional/public finance → operating budgets
prerequisites: Clear owner for operations; evidence from pilots
evidence_available: Examples of large approved programmes; claimed catalytic role of grants (self-reported)
evidence_thin: Attribution of public finance to earlier grants; who pays O&M after pilots
decisive_questions: Who pays operating costs in year 3, and is it in a budget?
learning_agenda_12_24m: Trace two pilots from grant to public budget; document O&M commitments
risks_and_distribution: Double-counting catalytic claims; pilots that end with the grant
exit_and_sustainability: Operating costs in public budgets or user fees
what_would_change_my_mind: If no pilot secures an operating budget within three years
